title: A Spread of Ratios Lowers Arterial Oxygen

scenes.tts: A resting adult moves roughly six litres of air and five litres of blood through the lungs every minute. Do those two numbers tell you what the blood leaves with? They do not. What settles it is whether air and blood arrive at the same places in the same proportion.
scenes.visual: Air and blood flow into a lung block; the question mark; per-unit air and blood bars.
scenes.narration: A resting adult moves roughly six litres of air and five litres of blood through the lungs every minute. Do those two numbers tell you what the blood leaves with? They do not. What settles it is whether air and blood arrive at the same places in the same proportion.

scenes.tts: For a given inspired gas and mixed venous blood, one quantity mainly sets a unit's gas. That quantity is its ventilation divided by its perfusion. At a ratio of zero, a unit is perfused and not ventilated, which makes it a shunt. Its blood leaves with the oxygen content it arrived with. At an infinite ratio, a unit is ventilated and not perfused, which makes it dead space.
scenes.visual: Ratio number line; shunt unit at zero, dead space unit at infinity.
scenes.narration: For a given inspired gas and mixed venous blood, one quantity mainly sets a unit's gas. That quantity is its ventilation divided by its perfusion. At a ratio of zero, a unit is perfused and not ventilated, which makes it a shunt. Its blood leaves with the oxygen content it arrived with. At an infinite ratio, a unit is ventilated and not perfused, which makes it dead space.

scenes.tts: Real lungs hold a spread of ratios, which an inert-gas method recovers. In four young semirecumbent normal subjects, 95.5 percent of both blood flow and ventilation lay between ratios of 0.3 and 2.1. There was no shunt on air. Reference values for healthy people put the mean of the blood-flow distribution at 0.80 to 1.00. Textbooks quote a single whole-lung ratio of 0.8. That is not the same as the mean of a measured distribution.

scenes.tts: A spread lowers arterial P O two by itself. That holds even when every unit equilibrates with its own alveolar gas. The two averages are taken differently. Expired alveolar gas is weighted by ventilation, so well-ventilated units dominate it. Arterial blood is weighted by blood flow, so poorly ventilated units count for more in it.

scenes.tts: Blood from different units then mixes by oxygen content, not by partial pressure. Content is how much oxygen each decilitre of blood carries. The oxygen dissociation curve, which plots content against partial pressure, is flat at the top. So a high-ratio unit adds almost nothing per decilitre. A low-ratio unit subtracts a great deal.
scenes.visual: Schematic saturating curve; dot moves right (little gain) and left (large loss).

scenes.tts: Alveolar P O two is calculated, not measured. The result is an alveolar-arterial oxygen difference, even when every unit equilibrates with its own alveolar gas. It is a difference, not a diffusion gradient. Each unit's ratio mainly sets its gas, for a given inspired gas and mixed venous blood. A spread of ratios alone can widen the alveolar-arterial difference.
